title: Performance Engineering and Capacity Planning
objectives: Design for performance and plan capacity in government-scale services
Define meaningful performance budgets and SLOs for government services
Apply performance testing strategies appropriate to each delivery phase
Distinguish between performance problems caused by architecture versus implementation
Plan capacity for predictable peaks and unpredictable demand surges
whyThisMatters:
Government services experience demand patterns unlike most private sector systems. Self Assessment tax returns create a predictable peak every January where HMRC processes millions of submissions in a single week. Universal Credit creates sustained high demand every working day. A ministerial announcement about a new grant scheme can send traffic from zero to 100,000 users within hours without warning.

Performance failures in government are not just commercial losses — they prevent citizens from accessing services they are legally entitled to, generate public anger and political scrutiny, and undermine trust in digital government. When HMRC's systems slow during the Self Assessment deadline, it makes national news. When a visa system cannot handle post-pandemic demand, it creates real hardship.

Performance is an architecture concern, not just a tuning concern. A system with fundamental architectural bottlenecks — synchronous processing of high-volume requests, a single database handling all traffic, or a chatty integration requiring dozens of API calls per page load — cannot be made fast through implementation optimisation alone. The architecture must be designed for the required performance from the start.

content.heading: Performance as an Architecture Decision
content.body:
Every architecture decision has performance implications. Some decisions create performance ceilings that no amount of optimisation can overcome. Others create performance foundations that enable the system to scale gracefully.

Synchronous versus asynchronous processing: a service that processes every request synchronously — waiting for each downstream call to complete before responding — creates a performance ceiling determined by the slowest downstream dependency. If your payment service takes 3 seconds and your notification service takes 2 seconds and both are called synchronously per request, your minimum response time is 5 seconds regardless of how fast your own code runs. Asynchronous processing (queue the payment, queue the notification, respond immediately) removes this ceiling.

Database architecture: a single relational database handling all reads and writes for all functions creates a contention bottleneck. Read replicas, caching layers, CQRS (separating read and write models), and domain-specific data stores remove this bottleneck by distributing load across multiple resources.

Caching strategy: every piece of data that can be served from cache rather than computed fresh is a performance win multiplied by every request. But caching introduces consistency challenges — how stale can cached data be? Architecture decisions about caching determine your performance envelope: a service with aggressive caching handles 100x the load of one without, but at the cost of data freshness.

API design: chatty APIs (requiring many calls to compose a single page) multiply latency. Each call adds network round-trip time, serialisation overhead, and potential for failure. APIs designed for the consumer's needs — returning the right data in the right shape in a single call — reduce both latency and failure probability.

Stateless service design: stateless services (no in-memory session state) can be horizontally scaled by simply adding more instances behind a load balancer. Stateful services require sticky sessions or distributed state management, both of which limit scaling options and add complexity.

These are architecture decisions made early in design. Getting them wrong creates performance problems that cannot be fixed without restructuring. Getting them right creates a system that performs well naturally and scales predictably.

content.heading: Defining Performance Requirements for Government Services
content.body:
Performance requirements must be specific, measurable, and grounded in user needs — not in technical ambition.

Response time targets should reflect user expectations and task context. For citizen-facing interactive services, the GDS Service Standard implies responsiveness — pages should load quickly enough that users do not abandon. Research consistently shows that user satisfaction degrades sharply above 3 seconds. For internal caseworker tools used all day, even 1-second delays compound into significant productivity loss across thousands of daily interactions. For APIs consumed by other services, response time affects the consumer's own performance — agree SLOs (Service Level Objectives) collaboratively.

Throughput targets should reflect realistic demand modelling. How many concurrent users will the service support? What is the normal daily transaction volume? What is the peak — and when does it occur? Government services often have predictable peaks: tax deadlines, benefit payment days, term-time application windows, end-of-financial-year reporting. Model these explicitly.

Availability targets (covered in lesson 24) interact with performance — a service that is technically available but responding in 30 seconds is effectively unavailable to users.

Performance budgets decompose the total acceptable response time into budgets for each component. If your target is 3 seconds end-to-end, and the network accounts for 500ms, the CDN for 200ms, and the server processing for 1000ms, you have 1300ms budget remaining for database queries, downstream API calls, and rendering. If any component exceeds its budget, the total target is breached. Budgets make performance allocation explicit and prevent individual components from consuming more than their share.

SLOs (Service Level Objectives) define what 'good enough' looks like in measurable terms. Examples: 'P95 response time under 2 seconds' (95% of requests complete within 2 seconds), 'error rate below 0.1%' (fewer than 1 in 1000 requests fail), 'throughput of 500 requests per second sustained' (the system can handle this load continuously). SLOs should be agreed with the service owner and monitored continuously.

content.heading: Performance Testing Strategy
content.body:
Performance testing validates that the architecture and implementation meet performance requirements under realistic conditions. Different types of performance test answer different questions.

Load testing applies expected production load to the system and measures response times, throughput, and resource utilisation. It answers: does the system meet its performance targets under normal conditions? Conduct load testing in beta once the architecture is stable and the main user journeys are implemented.

Stress testing applies load beyond expected levels — typically 2-3x normal peak — to find the breaking point. It answers: at what load does the system degrade? How does it degrade — gradually (response times increasing) or catastrophically (errors, crashes, data loss)? Stress testing reveals whether your graceful degradation mechanisms work.

Spike testing simulates sudden demand surges — zero to peak in seconds. It answers: can the system handle a sudden influx (a ministerial announcement, a deadline reminder, a media mention)? Does auto-scaling react quickly enough? Are there cold-start problems (first requests after scaling are slow because caches are empty)?

Soak testing runs sustained load over extended periods (hours or days). It answers: are there memory leaks, connection pool exhaustion, or other problems that only manifest over time? A system that performs well for 10 minutes may degrade over 48 hours as resources leak.

Performance testing in government has specific considerations. Test environments must be representative of production — same infrastructure configuration, same data volumes (or realistic synthetic data), same network topology. Testing against a scaled-down environment produces meaningless results because the bottlenecks are different. If production runs on 4 instances behind a load balancer with a multi-GB database, test against a similar configuration — not a single instance with an empty database.

The Service Standard expects evidence of performance testing at live assessment. Assessors will ask: what load was tested? Was it representative of expected production load? What were the results? What happens at peak? This evidence should accumulate through beta, not be produced in a last-minute exercise.

content.heading: Capacity Planning for Government Demand Patterns
content.body:
Government services have distinctive demand patterns that require specific capacity planning approaches.

Predictable peaks: many government services have known peak periods. Self Assessment peaks in January. Student finance peaks in September. Flood warnings peak during winter storms. Grant applications peak at deadline dates. For these services, capacity must be planned for the peak, not the average — and the infrastructure must be able to scale to peak capacity when needed.

Cloud auto-scaling helps but has limitations. Scaling takes time (minutes for new instances to start and warm up). Databases do not scale horizontally as easily as application servers. Downstream dependencies may not scale with you. Plan auto-scaling with sufficient headroom and tested scaling triggers — do not rely on it to handle instantaneous spikes.

Unpredictable surges: some demand is genuinely unpredictable. A ministerial announcement about a new scheme, a media report about a deadline, or a social media campaign can drive traffic from baseline to 100x within minutes. Architecture for unpredictable surges requires: CDN for static content (absorbs the majority of surge traffic without hitting your application), queue-based processing for submissions (accept requests into a queue and process asynchronously — the queue absorbs the spike while processing continues at a sustainable rate), and rate limiting (protect downstream systems by limiting how many requests are forwarded per second, serving a 'service is busy' page to excess requests).

Capacity modelling for government services should consider: current user base and transaction volumes, growth projections (user base increasing, transaction frequency increasing), known future events (deadlines, policy changes that will drive demand), and worst-case scenarios (what happens if demand is 10x projection due to an unexpected event?).

The cost dimension: capacity costs money. In cloud environments, you pay for what you provision. Over-provisioning for extreme peaks that rarely occur wastes public money. Under-provisioning for peaks that definitely occur creates service failures. The architecture decision is: what is the right balance between cost and resilience? For critical services, over-provision. For non-critical services, accept graceful degradation during extreme peaks.

content.heading: Diagnosing Performance Problems: Architecture vs Implementation
content.body:
When a service is slow, the first question is: is this an architecture problem or an implementation problem? The distinction matters because the fix is completely different.

Architecture problems are structural. They cannot be fixed by optimising code — they require changing how the system is composed. Examples: synchronous calls to slow dependencies (fix: make them asynchronous), all traffic hitting a single database (fix: read replicas or caching), N+1 query patterns from the API design (fix: redesign the API to return related data in a single call), and chatty inter-service communication (fix: coarser-grained API boundaries).

Implementation problems are within components. They can be fixed without changing the architecture. Examples: inefficient database queries (fix: add indexes, optimise queries), unnecessary computation (fix: cache computed results), large response payloads (fix: pagination, filtering, compression), and memory leaks (fix: identify and fix the leak).

Diagnostic approach:

First, identify where time is being spent. Use distributed tracing (correlation IDs through all services) to see the breakdown: how much time in each component, how much in network transit, how much waiting for downstream services? This reveals whether the bottleneck is architectural (time split across many downstream calls) or implementation (time concentrated in one component).

Second, check if the problem scales linearly or exponentially with load. Linear degradation (response time increases proportionally with load) suggests a capacity problem — add resources. Exponential degradation (response time accelerates as load increases) suggests a contention problem — lock contention, connection pool exhaustion, or a serialisation bottleneck.

Third, check whether the problem exists at low load. If the system is slow with a single user, it is an implementation problem. If it is fast with a single user but slow under load, it is a concurrency or scaling problem — potentially architectural.

For architects, the critical skill is recognising architecture problems early — ideally before they manifest in production. Review your architecture for known bottleneck patterns during design. Challenge any architecture where all traffic passes through a single component, where response time depends on the number of downstream calls, or where scaling one component does not proportionally increase throughput.

content.heading: Performance in the Government Technology Stack
content.body:
Government services typically use a predictable technology stack. Understanding the performance characteristics of common government architecture components helps you make informed decisions.

GOV.UK Frontend and Design System: the GOV.UK Design System is designed for performance — minimal JavaScript, server-side rendering, progressive enhancement. Services using it correctly are fast by default. Performance problems with GOV.UK-style services typically come from the backend, not the frontend.

Cloud managed services: most government cloud deployments use managed services (managed databases, managed container orchestration, managed message queues). These handle their own scaling and performance — but within limits defined by your configuration tier. Ensure your tier is appropriate for your load, and monitor to detect when you are approaching tier limits.

GOV.UK Notify: a shared platform with its own capacity. Your service depends on Notify's performance for sending communications. Design for Notify being occasionally slow or unavailable — queue notifications and retry, rather than blocking user-facing operations on notification delivery.

GOV.UK Pay: similarly, a dependency with its own performance characteristics. Payment processing should be asynchronous from the user's perspective where possible — submit the payment request, show the user a confirmation, and reconcile payment success asynchronously.

Integration with legacy systems: this is typically the biggest performance constraint in government architectures. Legacy systems often have limited throughput, unpredictable response times, and no ability to scale. Architecture patterns for legacy integration performance include: caching frequently-requested data locally (reducing calls to legacy), asynchronous batch integration (exchanging data in batches rather than real-time), and queue-based buffering (smoothing demand spikes so legacy receives a steady stream rather than bursts).

Content Delivery Networks (CDN): for any service with static content (images, stylesheets, JavaScript, downloadable documents), a CDN dramatically improves performance and absorbs traffic spikes. GOV.UK uses Fastly as its CDN. For departmental services, ensure static assets are served through a CDN and configured with appropriate cache headers.

workedExample.title: Capacity Planning for a DESNZ Grant Scheme Launch
workedExample.context: DESNZ is launching a new energy efficiency grant scheme for homeowners. Based on eligibility criteria, approximately 2 million households qualify. The minister will announce the scheme on national television during a prime-time news bulletin. Past experience with similar schemes suggests 10-15% of eligible households will attempt to access the service within the first 24 hours, with 50% of those in the first 2 hours after announcement. The service must remain responsive (sub-3-second page loads) throughout the surge. The scheme opens for applications immediately after the announcement.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect models the expected demand and designs the architecture to handle it.

Demand modelling:
- Eligible households: 2 million
- First 24 hours: 200,000-300,000 visitors (10-15%)
- First 2 hours: 100,000-150,000 visitors (50% of day-one traffic)
- Peak concurrent users: estimated 25,000-40,000 (based on session duration of 15 minutes)
- Page views per session: estimated 8 (eligibility check, form pages, submission)
- Peak requests per second: approximately 3,000-5,000

Architecture for peak demand:
- CDN: all static assets (CSS, JS, images, guidance pages) served from CDN edge. This absorbs 70%+ of raw traffic before it reaches the application.
- Application tier: auto-scaling group configured to scale from 4 instances (baseline) to 40 instances (peak), triggered at 70% CPU utilisation. Pre-warming: 20 instances launched 1 hour before announcement.
- Eligibility check: stateless, cacheable for identical inputs. Results cached for 1 hour (eligibility criteria do not change during that period).
- Form submission: asynchronous processing. The user receives immediate confirmation, and the application is queued for backend processing. This decouples the user experience from backend capacity.
- Database: read replicas for eligibility checks and status queries. Write operations (submissions) go to primary. Connection pooling configured for peak concurrent connections.
- GOV.UK Notify: confirmation emails queued and sent asynchronously. Do not block the submission response on email delivery.

Performance testing plan:
- Week -4: load test at expected peak (5,000 RPS). Identify and fix bottlenecks.
- Week -2: stress test at 2x peak (10,000 RPS). Verify graceful degradation.
- Week -1: spike test simulating instantaneous surge (0 to 5,000 RPS in 60 seconds). Verify auto-scaling and cache warming.
- Day -1: smoke test in production at low load to verify production configuration matches test environment.

Graceful degradation plan:
If demand exceeds 2x projection (extreme scenario): enable rate limiting at the CDN layer, serving a 'service is busy, please try again in 30 minutes' page to excess requests. This protects the application tier from overload. Users are never told the service is unavailable — only that it is busy.
workedExample.outcome: The announcement drives 280,000 visitors in the first 24 hours (within the modelled range). Peak concurrent users reach 35,000. The architecture handles the load without degradation — page load times remain under 2 seconds throughout. The pre-warming decision proves critical: without it, auto-scaling would have taken 4-5 minutes to respond, during which early users would have experienced slow responses. The asynchronous submission processing means the 280,000 visits do not create 280,000 concurrent database write operations — submissions are processed steadily over the following hours.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The key decisions were: pre-warming (not relying on reactive auto-scaling for a known spike), asynchronous submission (decoupling user experience from backend processing), and aggressive CDN caching (keeping the majority of traffic away from the application tier). The demand modelling was close to reality because it was based on previous comparable scheme launches — historical data from similar services is the most reliable input to capacity planning.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Service That Collapsed on Deadline Day
civilServiceScenario.background: A government regulatory service requires annual submissions from 50,000 businesses by 31 March each year. Historically, 60% of businesses submit in the final week, and 30% submit on the final day. This year, the service experienced severe degradation from 2pm on 31 March — response times exceeded 30 seconds, and many users received timeout errors. Approximately 8,000 businesses could not submit by the deadline. The minister has received complaints from trade associations and is facing parliamentary questions.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: As the Solution Architect, you must: (1) identify the root cause of the failure, (2) propose immediate mitigation for next year, and (3) recommend architecture changes that prevent recurrence permanently.
constraints: The service is monolithic — a single application handling all functions
The database is a single instance with no read replicas
There is no CDN — all requests hit the application directly
The submission process is synchronous — it validates, processes, and stores before responding
Auto-scaling is not configured — the service runs on fixed infrastructure
No load testing was conducted before the deadline
The service has a budget of £80,000 for improvements
The architecture must not be fully redesigned — incremental improvement only
The next deadline is in 12 months
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect conducting the post-incident analysis and proposing improvements.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This is a classic government performance failure: predictable peak demand meeting an architecture designed for average demand. The root cause is architectural — a monolithic application with a single database and no scaling capability was never going to handle 15,000+ concurrent users on deadline day.

Within £80,000 and 12 months, full architectural redesign is not feasible. But targeted improvements can prevent recurrence: add a CDN for static content (immediately reduces application load), add a database read replica (eligibility checks and status queries can use the replica), implement connection pooling, configure auto-scaling for the application tier, add a queue for submission processing (accept the submission immediately, process asynchronously), and conduct load testing 4 weeks before next deadline.

The longer-term lesson: services with known demand peaks must be performance-tested at peak volumes before they go live. This failure was preventable with a £5,000 load test that would have revealed the bottleneck months in advance.

practiceArtefact.description: Conduct a performance architecture review of the following proposed design: A citizen-facing service will process 200,000 applications per year. The architecture is: React frontend → API gateway → Application service → PostgreSQL database. The application service makes synchronous calls to 3 downstream APIs (identity verification, address lookup, payment processing) during form submission. Expected peak: 5,000 concurrent users during a 2-week application window. Identify performance risks and propose mitigations.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider: what is the critical path for a form submission? Where are the potential bottlenecks? What happens when a downstream API is slow? What is the peak request rate and can the architecture handle it? Propose specific architectural changes for each identified risk.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Performance Architecture Review: Application Processing Service**

**Critical Path Analysis:**
Form submission: Frontend → API Gateway → Application Service → (Identity API + Address API + Payment API sequentially) → Database write → Response
Estimated critical path time: 200ms (app) + 2000ms (identity) + 500ms (address) + 3000ms (payment) + 100ms (DB) = 5800ms minimum

**Risk 1: Sequential Downstream Calls (HIGH)**
Three synchronous downstream API calls in sequence create a minimum 5.5-second response time. If any API is slow, the total response time increases linearly.
Impact: User waits 6+ seconds for submission confirmation. At peak load with 5,000 concurrent users, application threads are consumed waiting for downstream responses.
Mitigation: Parallelise independent calls (identity and address can run simultaneously — reducing path by 500ms). Make payment asynchronous (accept submission immediately, process payment in background, notify user of payment result via GOV.UK Notify).
Revised path: 200ms + max(2000ms, 500ms) + 100ms = 2300ms (excluding async payment)

**Risk 2: Single Database Instance (MEDIUM)**
All reads and writes hit a single PostgreSQL instance. At peak (5,000 concurrent users, 8 pages per session), read load will be approximately 2,000 queries/second.
Impact: Database becomes the bottleneck under peak load. Query latency increases, causing cascading slowness.
Mitigation: Add a read replica for all read queries (status checks, form pre-population). Connection pooling to manage concurrent connections. Database connection limit: ensure pool size matches expected concurrent application instances.

**Risk 3: No Caching Layer (MEDIUM)**
Eligibility rules, reference data (address lookups), and form configuration are fetched from the database on every request.
Impact: Unnecessary database load for data that changes infrequently.
Mitigation: Add an in-memory cache (Redis) for: eligibility rules (cache for 1 hour), address lookup results (cache for 24 hours), form configuration (cache until explicitly invalidated). Expected cache hit rate: 80%+, reducing database read load by 80%.

**Risk 4: Downstream API Failure (MEDIUM)**
If the identity verification API is unavailable, the entire submission path fails.
Impact: Complete service outage for a third-party dependency outside your control.
Mitigation: Circuit breaker pattern on all downstream calls. For identity: queue submissions for later verification if identity API is unavailable (verify within 24 hours). For address: cache previous lookups, use cached result if API is down. For payment: already asynchronous in revised design.

**Risk 5: No Auto-Scaling (HIGH)**
Fixed infrastructure cannot absorb the difference between baseline (200 users) and peak (5,000 users).
Impact: Infrastructure saturated at peak, causing degradation or failure.
Mitigation: Configure auto-scaling from 2 instances (baseline) to 20 instances (peak). Set scaling trigger at 60% CPU utilisation. Pre-warm to 10 instances at the start of the application window.

**Summary:** Three architecture changes are essential before peak: (1) asynchronous payment processing, (2) auto-scaling, (3) caching layer. Two are highly recommended: (4) parallelised downstream calls, (5) read replica.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the last performance problem you encountered. Was it caused by an architecture decision or an implementation issue? How did you determine which?
Does your service have defined SLOs for response time, throughput, and availability? If not, how do you know whether performance is acceptable?
When did you last performance test your service at realistic peak load? If the answer is 'never' or 'at launch only,' what risks does that create?
How would you handle a situation where meeting a performance requirement conflicts with meeting a functional requirement? What trade-offs would you consider?
Think about a government service with known demand peaks. How would you design differently for a service where 80% of annual usage occurs in one week versus one where demand is uniform?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common architectural cause of performance problems in government services?
options: Using cloud hosting instead of on-premise servers
Synchronous calls to multiple downstream dependencies creating cumulative latency
Using the GOV.UK Design System for the frontend
Storing data in relational databases
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Synchronous sequential calls to downstream APIs create cumulative latency — each dependency's response time adds to the total. A service calling 3 APIs sequentially at 2 seconds each has a minimum 6-second response time regardless of how fast its own code runs. The fix is parallelisation or asynchronous processing.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of performance budgets?
options: To set the financial budget for performance testing
To allocate acceptable response time portions to each component so no single component exceeds its share
To limit the number of users who can access the service
To determine how many servers to provision
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Performance budgets decompose the total acceptable response time into allocations for each component (network, CDN, application, database, downstream APIs). This makes the allocation explicit and prevents any single component from consuming more than its fair share of the total budget.

knowledgeCheck.question: What type of performance testing validates that a system handles sudden demand surges?
options: Load testing at expected average traffic
Soak testing over extended periods
Spike testing with instantaneous traffic increases
Unit testing of individual components
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Spike testing simulates sudden demand surges (0 to peak in seconds) and validates whether the system can handle instantaneous traffic increases — such as those caused by ministerial announcements or deadline reminders. It tests auto-scaling responsiveness, cache warming, and cold-start behaviour.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective architecture pattern for handling unpredictable demand surges?
options: Provisioning maximum possible infrastructure at all times
Queue-based asynchronous processing that decouples acceptance from processing
Blocking all traffic above a certain threshold
Redirecting excess traffic to a manual paper process
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Queue-based processing accepts requests immediately (maintaining good user experience) and processes them at a sustainable rate regardless of arrival rate. The queue absorbs the spike while backend processing continues steadily. This decouples the user's experience from backend capacity constraints.

knowledgeCheck.question: How should you determine performance requirements for a government service?
options: Use industry benchmarks from private sector applications
Base them on user needs, expected demand patterns, and the consequences of poor performance
Match the performance of the legacy system being replaced
Set them as low as possible to reduce infrastructure costs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Performance requirements should be grounded in: user expectations (how fast do users need the service to be?), demand modelling (how many concurrent users and what peak patterns?), and consequence analysis (what happens if performance degrades — user abandonment, missed deadlines, political scrutiny?). These factors determine what 'good enough' means for each specific service.
